---
title: "BiP-PRISM"
---

## What makes core-loss EELS expensive

A core-loss STEM-EELS simulation is a double-channelling problem. The probe has to
be propagated dynamically *to* an atom that ionizes, the ionization event has to be
applied there, and the inelastically scattered wave has to be propagated
dynamically *from* that atom to the detector. Both legs are multislice.

Written out, the conventional transition-potential multislice does this for every
combination of scan position, ionized atom and transition channel. With $P$ scan
positions, $N_a$ atoms of the ionized element and $N_t$ channels, that is
$P N_a N_t$ exit-wave propagations. The scan is the painful factor: it is the one
that grows when you ask for the atomic-resolution map you actually wanted.

## The scattering matrix removes the scan

PRISM's idea is that the entrance leg does not depend on where the probe is. A
converged probe is a sum of plane waves over the aperture, and multislice is
linear, so propagating each of the $B$ aperture beams once gives a basis
$\mathcal{S}_1$ from which the probe at *any* scan position is recovered as a
linear combination — the coefficients are the aperture's phase ramps. One
propagation of $B$ columns replaces $P$ propagations of one probe.

The exit leg yields to the same argument, and this is the step that makes
detector-integrated maps cheap. Everything after the transition potential is
linear too, so

$$
\psi_{\text{exit}}(\boldsymbol{\rho}) \;=\;
\mathcal{S}_2\Big[\,H_{n0}\sum_b c_b(\boldsymbol{\rho})\,\mathcal{S}_{1,b}\Big]
\;=\;
\sum_b c_b(\boldsymbol{\rho})\;\mathcal{S}_2\big[\,H_{n0}\,\mathcal{S}_{1,b}\big] .
$$

The expensive operator acts on the $B$ columns, not on the $P$ probes, and the
scan is synthesised afterwards by the same coefficients that formed it. For a
detector-integrated map $\mathcal{S}_2$ can be built once per slice as a
*transpose* multislice of the detector-accepted output beams — by reciprocity,
running the detector backwards is the same calculation as running the source
forwards — and then reused across every atom in that slice. The per-scan exit
propagation disappears entirely. This is the dual-matrix algorithm of Brown,
Ciston & Ophus.

## What is left is memory

Having traded time for structure, the cost reappears as storage. $\mathcal{S}_1$
is $B$ complex arrays on the full $N \times N$ grid; $\mathcal{S}_2$ is $n_{\text{det}}$
of them, and the detector is usually the wider aperture of the two. Both are
resident. On the FePt nanoparticle below, the exact dual matrix needs 63 GB — more
than any consumer card, and more than most cluster cards.

## Partitioning both matrices

Beam partitioning attacks exactly this. Neighbouring beams in the aperture differ
only by a small tilt, so their columns, once de-tilted, are locally similar. Build
the matrix on a sparse set of $B_p \ll B$ *parent* beams, and reconstruct the
column you need for any beam by natural-neighbour interpolation of the parents —
de-tilt, combine with the interpolation weights, re-tilt.

The reconstruction is only ever needed **locally**, and that is the point. The
ionization operator $H_{n0}(\mathbf{r} - \boldsymbol{\tau})$ has sub-ångström
support around the atom at $\boldsymbol{\tau}$, so it *is* the crop: the columns
only have to be right inside a small window, never across the whole grid.

**BiP-PRISM** — bi-partitioned PRISM — applies this to both matrices at once:
$\mathcal{S}_1$ on parent aperture beams, $\mathcal{S}_2$ on parent detector
beams, each reconstructed on the crop window around the ionized atom immediately
before the contraction

$$
\big[\mathcal{S}H_{n0}\big]_{db}
\;=\;
\sum_{\mathbf{r}\,\in\,\Omega_\tau}
\mathcal{S}_{2,d}(\mathbf{r})\,H_{n0}(\mathbf{r}-\boldsymbol{\tau})\,\mathcal{S}_{1,b}(\mathbf{r}) .
$$

Both reconstructions resolve *before* the contraction, on the window, and the
window is small — so the resident matrices shrink from $B$ and $n_{\text{det}}$
columns to $B_p$ each, while the arithmetic that consumes them is unchanged.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why the 4D cube only partitions $\mathcal{S}_1$

`prism_transition_potential` keeps the full exit diffraction pattern, so it makes
no detector reduction and $\mathcal{S}_2$ never becomes a matrix to partition — it
stays an on-the-fly multislice of the column basis. `partition` there applies to
$\mathcal{S}_1$ alone; `interpolation_factor` is the lever for the exit leg. Only
the detector-integrated map (`prism_eels_image`) has two matrices to partition,
and that is where the large savings are.
:::

## The locality result, and when it fails

Because the reconstruction is used only where $H_{n0}$ is non-zero, the error of
the whole simulation is governed entirely by the reconstruction error *on the
atom*. Nothing else in the algorithm approximates anything: the parent
propagations are exact multislice, the contraction is exact, the scan synthesis is
exact. This is what makes the approximation predictable rather than merely
empirical — there is one quantity to watch, and it is local.

The paper characterises this by sweeping a single column's conditions against an
exact-PRISM oracle, and the consequences are narrower than one might guess:

**Thickness is the binding failure mode.** The on-atom reconstruction error grows
with the propagation distance the parents have travelled before the ionization
plane, and the map error tracks it. Deep atoms in thick specimens are where more
parents are needed.

**Defocus and edge choice are not.** Cube and map error stay near 1% out to 200 Å
of defocus, and across edges from O-K to Cu-L. An earlier reading of the on-atom
diagnostic suggested defocus was a failure mode; that turned out to be an artefact
of the fixed diagnostic box — a defocused probe delocalises out of it and collapses
the normalisation. The full-grid error is stable, so the box diagnostic is an
in-focus instrument while the method itself tolerates defocus.

## Accuracy, and the one caveat worth knowing

Increasing the parent count reduces the error monotonically toward the exact
result, but the two kinds of error do not converge at the same rate.

*Pattern* fidelity is excellent almost immediately. *Absolute scale* converges
more slowly, and the reason is coherent: the de-tilted parent columns are combined
as complex numbers, and averaging phases that have partly decohered gives
$|\sum_p w_p T_p| < \sum_p w_p |T_p|$, so the reconstruction loses amplitude.

Measured here on a Ti-L map of a 6×6×16-cell SrTiO₃ slab (256² grid, 576 ionized
atoms, 64² scan), against the exact dual matrix at the same interpolation factor:

| | Correlation | Intensity vs exact | Scale-normalised RMS |
|---|---|---|---|
| `n_radial=2` | 0.980 | 0.51× | 0.17 |
| `n_radial=4` | 0.987 | 0.61× | 0.14 |
| `n_radial=8` | 0.9997 | 0.95× | 0.02 |

At sparse partitions the map is pattern-faithful and roughly a factor of two too
small. Splitting the two sides at `n_radial=4` shows where that comes from:

| | Correlation | Intensity vs exact |
|---|---|---|
| $\mathcal{S}_1$ only | 0.99997 | 0.97× |
| $\mathcal{S}_2$ only | 0.987 | 0.63× |

Essentially all of it is the detector matrix. $\mathcal{S}_2$ is back-propagated
through the remaining thickness, which makes its columns far harder to
interpolate than the probe-side ones, so it is the side to spend parents on.

::: {.callout-important}
## Take relative maps at face value; scale-check absolute cross-sections

If you are comparing intensities *within* a map, or to experiment after
normalisation, the sparse partitions are fine. If you need an absolute
cross-section, raise `n_radial` — on the detector side first — until the total
signal stops moving, and check it against `partition=None` on a smaller cell.
`partition` and `partition_s2` take independent dictionaries precisely so you can
spend parents where they are needed.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Not the same fix as elastic PRISM

Pelz *et al.* recover the partitioning error in elastic 4D-STEM by
back-propagating to the probe-crossover plane before interpolating. That does not
transfer here.
The Fresnel propagator is unitary and commutes through the interpolation sum, so
back-propagation changes the reconstruction error by nothing measurable; the
elastic gain comes from the crop applied *at* the crossover plane, and the
EELS analogue of that crop is $H_{n0}$, which pins the contraction to the atom
plane instead.
:::

## What it buys, and when

Memory is the headline. On the FePt-nanoparticle Fe-L benchmark at 936² sampling,
the paper reports the exact dual matrix at 63 GB against 1.2–8 GB partitioned —
8–50×, and the difference between needing a cluster node and needing one card.
The *time* saving is more modest, typically a small factor, and that is structural
rather than disappointing: the per-atom window contraction is shared between the
exact and partitioned paths, so Amdahl's law caps what partitioning can do to the
runtime. What partitioning changes is the build, the residency, and therefore
which simulations are possible at all.

::: {.callout-warning}
## On a small problem, partitioning buys nothing

The saving is in the resident matrices, $B$ and $n_{\text{det}}$ columns of an
$N \times N$ grid each. They only dominate once the grid and the beam count are
large. On the SrTiO₃ slab above — 256², 793 aperture beams — peak memory is set by
the per-atom contraction intermediate instead, which partitioning does not touch,
and the measured result is 2.06 GB exact against 1.89–2.04 GB partitioned, with
the partitioned runs 10–15% *slower* from the reconstruction overhead.

Reach for `partition` when the matrices are what is filling the card. Below that,
use the exact path and get the exact answer.
:::
